sections.heading: What does heart failure feel like, and how does it progress?
sections.body:
Heart failure means the heart is struggling to pump blood around the body effectively. It does not mean the heart has stopped or is about to stop. Common symptoms include breathlessness during activity or when lying down, tiredness, swollen ankles and legs, and feeling lightheaded. Some people also have a cough that keeps coming back at night, or a fast heart rate.

Heart failure usually needs lifelong treatment and often gets worse over time, according to the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute. Fluid build-up can show as weight gain, swollen ankles or worsening breathlessness. Other signs of fluid build-up include swelling of the legs or abdomen, a worsening cough, trouble sleeping flat, dizziness and confusion.

sections.heading: What are the types of heart failure?
sections.body:
The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute describes left-sided heart failure as the more common form. It has two main types, which are named after the ejection fraction, a measure of how much blood the left side of the heart pumps out with each beat.

In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the left side of the heart is weak and cannot pump enough blood to the rest of the body. In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, the left side is too stiff to relax fully between heartbeats. The British Heart Foundation also describes a mildly reduced group that sits between these two.

Left-sided heart failure is the main cause of right-sided heart failure, and what starts on the left can progress to the right. Long-term, or chronic, heart failure is often caused by other medical conditions that damage or overwork the heart. Sudden, or acute, heart failure can be caused by an injury or infection that damages the heart, a heart attack or a blood clot in the lung.

sections.heading: How is heart failure diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP checks the symptoms and may arrange a blood test. NHS England advises GPs to arrange a natriuretic peptide blood test, called NT-proBNP, for people with suspected heart failure. The NICE guideline links the result to how soon a specialist assessment and an echocardiogram should happen, with higher results prompting faster referral.

If the blood test suggests heart failure, the GP refers the person to a specialist heart failure team, who may offer further tests. The NHS says these tests may include blood and urine samples, an electrocardiogram (ECG), scans such as a chest X-ray, echocardiogram and MRI scan, and tests to check the lungs. An echocardiogram is an ultrasound scan of the heart. NICE describes it as used to exclude important valve disease and to assess how well the left ventricle, the main pumping chamber, works.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for heart failure?
sections.body:
The NHS says medicines are the main treatment for heart failure, and that surgery may help some people. It also describes lifestyle changes as a core part of care. Treatment will usually be needed for life, and people often take two or three different medicines.

Some people have an implanted device. The most common is a cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) device, and versions that also include a defibrillator are usually called CRT-Ds. Surgical options include heart valve surgery, left ventricular assist devices and heart transplant. The NHS says a heart transplant may be offered if other treatments are not helping.

The NHS states that everyone diagnosed with heart failure should be offered cardiac rehabilitation, which is a programme that includes exercise.

sections.heading: What is it like living with heart failure?
sections.body:
Daily weight checks help to spot fluid build-up early. A healthy diet, staying active, not smoking and keeping to a healthy weight all help. One NHS hospital guide suggests limiting salt and not adding it at the table or in cooking. It advises drinking very little alcohol, and some people are advised to stop completely if alcohol contributed to the condition.

People with heart failure should be offered a flu vaccine every year and a one-off pneumococcal vaccine, the NHS says. The NHS also says monitoring should happen at least every six months.

Some people feel anxious, scared or depressed after a diagnosis. These feelings are common, and the GP or care team should be told if they make everyday life hard.

sections.heading: What is the outlook, and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
Nobody can predict exactly how long a person will live with heart failure. The outlook depends on the cause, age, symptoms and general health. Some people are at risk of sudden death from a dangerous heart rhythm. There is no cure in most cases, but treatment can control symptoms for many years and people can improve their quality of life.

The NHS advises seeing a GP about any symptoms of heart failure, and a routine GP appointment is the usual first step. It advises contacting a GP urgently or calling NHS 111 for sudden weight gain, or for breathlessness when lying down or during everyday activity. The NHS says to call 999 for severe difficulty breathing, pale or blue lips or skin, or if someone has passed out. It advises against driving to A&E in these situations.

faqs.q: Does heart failure mean the heart has stopped?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says heart failure means the heart is struggling to pump blood effectively, but it does not mean the heart has stopped or is about to stop. Treatment can control symptoms for many years in most cases, the NHS says.

In most cases there is no cure for heart failure. The NHS says treatment can control symptoms for many years. Options include lifestyle changes, medicines, implanted devices and surgery, and a clinician decides which suit each person. Treatment will usually be needed for life.

faqs.q: Will someone with heart failure need treatment for life?
faqs.a: The NHS says treatment will usually be needed for life. Medicines are the main treatment, and people often take two or three different types. Regular monitoring is part of care, and the NHS says it should happen at least every six months.

faqs.q: Who looks after people with heart failure?
faqs.a: A GP usually starts by checking symptoms and may arrange a blood test. If the result suggests heart failure, the GP refers the person to a specialist heart failure team. The British Heart Foundation and Pumping Marvellous offer information and community support.

faqs.q: Is exercise part of heart failure care?
faqs.a: The NHS says everyone diagnosed with heart failure should be offered cardiac rehabilitation. Exercise is part of that programme. A healthy diet, staying active, not smoking and a healthy weight are also described as helpful. People with heart failure should also be offered flu and pneumococcal vaccines, the NHS says.
